post.caption: Once, only two painite crystals were known. Arthur Pain recognized that a crystal from Burma was unusual, and it came from the gem gravels of Mogok in the early 1950s. In 1957 scientists announced a new mineral, painite, named for him. Its chemistry includes zirconium and boron, plus calcium and aluminum, and its color runs from red to brownish orange-red. A third crystal turned up in 1979, and in 2001 that extreme rarity began to change. Today over a thousand crystals are known, but few can be cut, and by 2004 only two faceted stones had reportedly been found. The original crystal is kept at London's Natural History Museum.
